content.text:
The folder `data/` holds the data behind a published data story, "The Diva-ness of 138 National Anthem Performances": https://pudding.cool/2024/02/anthems/
The files: data/src__data__ids.csv, data/src__data__pitch__desktop__full.csv

Write down the story's findings that this data reproduces.

1. Read the story on the web. web_fetch returns the page as the server sends it. web_view opens it in a browser and scrolls it like a reader, so it also gets text drawn by scripts, chart labels and the text of scrolling steps: use it when web_fetch returns little of the story, and to read what the charts label. Follow links to the story's methods or data notes when they say how a number was computed.
2. List every finding the authors draw from data: each number, comparison, ranking, share, trend or pattern the text states or a chart labels. A description of the data itself is not a finding: how many records, people, items, categories or sources it has, and how it was collected. When a chart states the same thing for each of its items (the top three for each phrase, the share for each year), that is one finding, written as one fact whose code computes it for every item at once.
3. Write each finding the files in data/ can reproduce as a fact in `facts.json`:

```json
[{"id": "women-front-shorter",
  "source": "On average, the pockets in women's jeans are 48% shorter and 6.5% narrower than men's pockets.",
  "claim": "Women's front pockets average 14.3 cm of maximum height against 23.1 cm for men.",
  "tables": {"m": "data/measurements.csv"},
  "code": "m.groupby('menWomen').maxHeightFront.mean()"}]
```

- `id`: unique in the file, a few meaningful words.
- `source`: the story's own words for this finding, quoted exactly, from its text or a chart label.
- `claim`: the finding in one sentence, with the numbers the code prints, and nothing the printout does not show: the story's own wording and numbers belong in `source`, not in the claim.
- `tables`: the files the code reads, each a variable name and the file's path from this folder, such as `data/orders.csv`; every file is read with `pd.read_csv(path)`.
- `code`: one Python expression over those variables, with `pd` (pandas) and `np` (numpy) available: the plain pandas computation whose printout shows the finding, such as a filter, a group-by, a count, a share or a sort. Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict.

Evaluate every fact from this folder the way it will be checked: read its `tables` with `pd.read_csv`, evaluate its `code`, print the value the way pandas prints it, and read the printout against the claim and the source. Every number, name and comparison in the claim must be in the printout, computed from the tables: code that writes a number itself, such as a string or a Series of typed-in values, does not count. The printout must agree with the story's numbers, up to rounding. Use the story's own definitions and filters, from its text or methods: a term means the same in every fact (if making it past the rookie contract is more than two seasons in one fact, it is more than two seasons in all of them), and a range, threshold or subset is one the story uses, never one chosen to make a number come out right. If the story's number only comes out under a definition or filter the story does not use, the finding is not reproduced. If after a fair try the data does not give the story's number (it needs other data, a different period, or the numbers differ beyond rounding), leave the finding out of facts.json.

4. Write `skipped.json`: every finding you left out, as [{"source": "the story's words", "why": "..."}].

Deliver both files, even when the data reproduces none of the story's findings: then `facts.json` is `[]`.
I'll start by looking at the data files and reading the story.

content.text:
Quantifying the Diva-ness of 138 National Anthem Performances
Skip to main content
Please rise and enable your audio for a stirring analysis of the United States
# National Anthem
By Jan Diehm and Michelle Pera-McGhee
Loading
When you think of legendary National Anthem performances, there’s a good chance Whitney Houston’s 1991 Super Bowl rendition comes to mind. More than 30 years later, and it’s still widely considered one of the best, if not the best, National Anthem performances of all time.
Then there’s Fergie’s viral performance from the 2018 NBA All-Star game. It’s also considered one of the most memorable National Anthem renditions, but for entirely different reasons.
The “Star Spangled Banner” has become a pop culture moment. Performers must make a calculated choice: stay classic and traditional or infuse it with flair. Maya Rudolph’s SNL performance is probably one of the most extreme paths you could choose.
Let’s look at the paths of nearly 140 performances from major political and sporting events. These lines track pitch (or frequency): the lower the line, the lower the notes and the higher the line, the higher the notes. We’ve transposed them all to the same key for easier comparison. Let’s zoom in and look at it one phrase at a time.
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Anthony Hamilton
Chaka Khan
Hunter Hayes
# Our picks
Amber Riley
We begin with “o say can you see.” Francis Scott Key penned this opening line after seeing the American flag flying defiantly over Fort McHenry having withstood a bombardment by British forces during the War of 1812.
The “Star Spangled Banner” didn’t become the US’ official anthem until nearly a century later in 1931, and it wasn’t thrust into the pop culture spotlight until the late 1960s when José Feliciano, Jimi Hendrix, and other stars started to put their spin on the standard melody .
It’s this spin we’re interested in, and to measure it we’ve created the Diva Score (nerdy details in the methods ). It quantifies how much a performance melodically deviates from the standard. For this first phrase, most performers keep it pretty simple like Amber Riley from 2010.
Using the Diva Score , we can go phrase by phrase and pick out the performers who were doing the most and those that made you say they “ ain’t no diva .” Click on the faces of the certified top divas (plus our picks) to hear their interpretation of each phrase.
Loading
# o say can you see
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Anthony Hamilton
Chris Stapleton
Lauren Alaina
Most performers don’t really get going until the last half of the song so these first few phrases are comparatively tame. But Anthony Hamilton — he’s basically singing a different melody at the 2019 NBA All-Star Game.
Loading
# by the dawn’s early light
Here, the phrases are ordered by average Diva Score instead of the order they are sung. The vocal fireworks start to explode around the “bombs are bursting in air.”
# Average Diva Score by Phrase
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Fantasia
Chaka Khan
Luke Bryan
# Our picks
Fergie
Let’s see how Fergie is doing. Her 2018 NBA All-Star Game performance is surprisingly tame Diva Score -wise. Sadly, the Diva Score can’t capture when someone manages to pronounce every single word in the weirdest, most sultry way possible.
Loading
# what so proudly we hailed
The NBA All-Star Game has been host to a lot of memorable national anthem performances — from Marvin Gaye to Fergie. Overall, basketball games yielded higher Diva Scores than other sporting events and political events.
# Average Diva Score by Event Type
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Anthony Hamilton
John Legend
Chris Stapleton
# Our picks
Scotty Mccreery
Taylor Swift
By looking at the pitch line, you can pick out artists’ signature shapes, like scooping into notes. This is a common technique for country stars like Chris Stapleton and Scotty McCreery .
Speaking of “country” stars, our dataset has two Taylor Swift performances — both (2006 and 2008) well before her pop shift. Back then she was just a kid with a guitar, so it’s understandable that she records some of the overall lowest Diva Scores (#114 and #129).
Loading
# at the twilight’s last gleaming
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Aretha Franklin
Usher
Marvin Gaye
# Our picks
Patti Labelle
T-Pain
Two words: Aretha Franklin . The “Queen of Soul” shows out on this phrase, and she’s in good company: 8 of the top 10 Diva Scores for this phrase are from fellow R&B artists.
Loading
# whose broad stripes and bright stars
Average Diva Scores by music genre match intuition, with R&B and pop divas adding more flourishes than country or rock divas.
# Average Diva Score by Music Genre
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Anthony Hamilton
John Oates
Marvin Gaye
# Our picks
Jazmine Sullivan
The Diva Score measures chaos, but it can’t tell if that chaos sounds good or bad. Case in point: Jazmine Sullivan rarely has a top 3 Diva Score (although she ranks as the #17 overall diva), but we think she consistently sings some of the most beautiful and creative vocal runs.
Loading
# through the perilous fight
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Chaka Khan
Marvin Gaye
Jewel
# Our picks
Christina Aguilera
Eric Burton
This phrase is a common trip up for performers like Christina Aguilera and Eric Burton , who both double back over previously sung phrases. After her gaffe, Aguilera said she hoped the “true spirit of [the] anthem still came through.” It did, X-Tina.
Loading
# o’er the ramparts we watched
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Anthony Hamilton
Eric Burton
T-Pain
Good anthem performances are rarely a given, but artists like Whitney, Beyoncé, and T-Pain make it look easy. Yes, you read that right, Mr. Autotune delivered a sterling rendition. This phrase was one of his top Diva Scores .
Loading
# were so gallantly streaming
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Chaka Khan
Patti Labelle
# Our picks
Steven Tyler
Trace Adkins
Jennifer Hudson
The “Star Spangled Banner” is treacherous to sing — start off too high and “you’re screwed.” Trace Adkins sings in the lowest key among our dataset (D); Jennifer Hudson (and others) are in the highest (A); and Steven Tyler sings just a step below that in G, by far the highest of any other man in our dataset.
Loading
# and the rocket’s red glare
F# (F sharp) is the most common key for women. It’s Bb (B flat) for men.
# Distribution of Musical Keys
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Chaka Khan
👑
# Our picks
H.E.R.
Taylor Swift
If you’ve been with us since the beginning, you’ll notice that Chaka Khan has racked up 5 top diva appearances in these first 9 phrases. She has the highest average Diva Score per phrase, making her our #1 Diva.
For slightly more mellow, but still noteworthy performances, check out H.E.R. at the 2023 World Series and Taylor Swift at the 2008 World Series, T-Swift's highest recorded Diva Score for a phrase.
Loading
# the bombs bursting in air
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Chris Stapleton
Demi Lovato
Peabo Bryson
# Our picks
Carrie Underwood
Some singers are National Anthem pros with 3 or more performances in our dataset. Carrie Underwood performed in 2010 , 2007 , 2006 , and 2017 , with all her renditions sounding nearly identical.
Meanwhile, Demi Lovato switches it up. They use unique vocal runs for each of their performances from 2012 , 2015 , and 2020 .
Loading
# gave proof through the night
There are 7 performers in our dataset who have performed the National Anthem 3 or more times. This is their intra- Diva Score , or how they compare to themselves.

Two inauguration performances, where “flag” is emphasized, rise to the top for this phrase: Beyoncé (2013) and Lady Gaga (2021) . We’ve seen a big evolution since Juanita Booker’s more traditional 1981 take.

Standard

Standard

# Our picks

Towards the end of the anthem, you’re not making the top diva list unless you have a well-deserved royalty nickname: “The Queen of Funk” Chaka Khan , “Queen of Hip-Hop Soul” Mary J. Blige , and the “Godmother of Soul” Patti Labelle .
Mary J. Blige, in particular, holds down two of the top 10 Diva Score spots for this phrase: her performances at the 2009 World Series and 2012 NBA All-Star Game .
Loading
# banner yet wave
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas
Nicole Scherzinger
Patti Labelle
Renée Fleming
# Our picks
Steven Tyler
Kristen Chenoweth
Remember, the Diva Score measures how different a performance is from the standard, so artists like Nicole Scherzinger and Steven Tyler who go up the octave and hit (well, sometimes hit) the high notes on “free” get bonus points.
Here, you can also see the really tight vibrato waves from classical- and Broadway-trained singers like Renee Fleming and Kristen Chenoweth .

Fergie
The true divas shine for the anthem’s closing phrase. Here are the top 10 Diva Scores . It’s pure chaos in the best way possible.

# and the home of the brave
o say can you see by the dawn’s early light what so proudly we hailed at the twilight’s last gleaming whose broad stripes and bright stars through the perilous fight o’er the ramparts we watched were so gallantly streaming and the rocket’s red glare the bombs bursting in air gave proof through the night that our flag was still there o say does that star spangled banner yet wave o’er the land of the free and the home of the brave
Skip to more data
Now that you know what to look and listen for in the “Star Spangled Banner,” it’s time to dive even further into the data. The heatmap below allows you to explore each of the 16 phrases for all 138 performances in our dataset. Surprisingly we didn’t get tired of listened to the anthem when doing this project, so maybe you won’t either!
If you want to hear more about our favorites, check us out on the Switched on Pop podcast .

# Methods
To build a catalog of celebrity National Anthem performances, we consulted several best-of lists , and collected performances from major sporting and political events like the Super Bowl, the World Series, and the presidential inauguration from 1980 on. We also included a few notable anthem performances prior to 1980.
We then set out to find a suitable audio/video recording of the performance on YouTube. We were able to find roughly 180 performances. Using a free online converter , we extracted mp3 audio files from each YouTube link. We then manually trimmed the

mp3 audio files so that they started right before the first word in the anthem and ended after the last. The trimmed audio was then uploaded to an AI-powered Vocal Remover program to isolate the vocals from the rest of the audio.
Once we had the isolated vocal files, we loaded them into Tony , an open source melody transcription tool developed by the Centre for Digital Music at Queen Mary, University of London. Along with 4 additional data assistants (Amel Awadelkarim, Dustin D’Andrea, Noah Fagan, and George McIntire), we listened to each vocal track, manually removed errant sounds (crowd noise, echos, jet flyovers, band accompaniments) and corrected pitch when necessary. Some performances were dropped at this stage due to poor audio quality.
We then exported the pitch data, which tracked frequency in Hz over time. We manually marked the starting and ending timestamps of each of the 16 phrases of the song. Some specific phrases for specific performances were also dropped at this stage due to poor audio quality. This process took over 100 hours of work and we couldn’t have done it without our data assistants, so thank you!
For each phrase, we used Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to compare it to the corresponding phrase in a “standard” performance of the National Anthem. DTW measures the similarity between two temporal sequences, neutralizing any variation in speed. In other words, it measures the amount a performer deviates from the standard, strictly melodically. This is what we called the Diva Score for each phrase. The Diva Score for a full performance was calculated by taking the average for all phrases from that performance. It’s not an exact science, but we think the Diva Scores match our intuition of what melodic Diva-ness is pretty closely!
Finally, thank you to our colleague Kevin Litman-Narvarro who originally planted the idea of looking into National Anthem performances.

# National Anthem
By Jan Diehm and Michelle Pera-McGhee
Loading
When you think of legendary National Anthem performances, there’s a good chance Whitney Houston’s 1991 Super Bowl rendition comes to mind. More than 30 years later, and it’s still widely considered one of the best, if not the best, National Anthem performances of all time.
Then there’s Fergie’s viral performance from the 2018 NBA All-Star game. It’s also considered one of the most memorable National Anthem renditions, but for entirely different reasons.
The “Star Spangled Banner” has become a pop culture moment. Performers must make a calculated choice: stay classic and traditional or infuse it with flair. Maya Rudolph’s SNL performance is probably one of the most extreme paths you could choose.
Let’s look at the paths of nearly 140 performances from major political and sporting events. These lines track pitch (or frequency): the lower the line, the lower the notes and the higher the line, the higher the notes. We’ve transposed them all to the same key for easier comparison. Let’s zoom in and look at it one phrase at a time.
Standard
Show divas
# Top divas

# Our picks
Amber Riley
We begin with “o say can you see.” Francis Scott Key penned this opening line after seeing the American flag flying defiantly over Fort McHenry having withstood a bombardment by British forces during the War of 1812.
The “Star Spangled Banner” didn’t become the US’ official anthem until nearly a century later in 1931, and it wasn’t thrust into the pop culture spotlight until the late 1960s when José Feliciano, Jimi Hendrix, and other stars started to put their spin on the standard melody .
It’s this spin we’re interested in, and to measure it we’ve created the Diva Score (nerdy details in the methods ). It quantifies how much a performance melodically deviates from the standard. For this first phrase, most performers keep it pretty simple like Amber Riley from 2010.
Using the Diva Score , we can go phrase by phrase and pick out the performers who were doing the most and those that made you say they “ ain’t no diva .” Click on the faces of the certified top divas (plus our picks) to hear their interpretation of each phrase.

Title: Quantifying the Diva-ness of 138 National Anthem Performances
URL Source: https://pudding.cool/2024/02/anthems/
Markdown Content:
We begin with “o say can you see.” Francis Scott Key penned this opening line after seeing the American flag flying defiantly over Fort McHenry having withstood a bombardment by British forces during the War of 1812.
The “Star Spangled Banner” didn’t become the US’ official anthem until nearly a century later in 1931, and it wasn’t thrust into the pop culture spotlight until the late 1960s when [José Feliciano,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aQkY2UFBUb4)[Jimi Hendrix,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sjzZh6-h9fM) and other stars started to put their spin on the .
It’s this spin we’re interested in, and to measure it we’ve created the **Diva Score** (nerdy details in the [methods](https://pudding.cool/2024/02/anthems/#methods)). It quantifies how much a performance melodically deviates from the standard. For this first phrase, most performers keep it pretty simple like from 2010.
Using the **Diva Score**, we can go phrase by phrase and pick out the performers who were doing the most and those that made you say they “[ain’t no diva](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rNM5HW13_O8%E2%80%8B%E2%80%8B).” Click on the faces of the certified top divas (plus our picks) to hear their interpretation of each phrase.
## o say can you see
Most performers don’t really get going until the last half of the song so these first few phrases are comparatively tame. But — he’s basically singing a different melody at the 2019 NBA All-Star Game.
## by the dawn’s early light
Here, the phrases are ordered by average **Diva Score** instead of the order they are sung. The vocal fireworks start to explode around the “bombs are bursting in air.”
### Average Diva Score by Phrase
Let’s see how is doing. Her 2018 NBA All-Star Game performance is surprisingly tame **Diva Score**-wise. Sadly, the **Diva Score** can’t capture when someone manages to pronounce every single word in the weirdest, most sultry way possible.
## what so proudly we hailed
The NBA All-Star Game has been host to a lot of memorable national anthem performances — from Marvin Gaye to Fergie. Overall, basketball games yielded higher **Diva Scores** than other sporting events and political events.
### Average Diva Score by Event Type
By looking at the pitch line, you can pick out artists’ signature shapes, like scooping into notes. This is a common technique for country stars like and .
Speaking of “country” stars, our dataset has two performances — both (2006 and 2008) well before her pop shift. Back then she was just a kid with a guitar, so it’s understandable that she records some of the overall lowest **Diva Scores** (#114 and #129).
## at the twilight’s last gleaming
Two words: . The “Queen of Soul” shows out on this phrase, and she’s in good company: 8 of the top 10 **Diva Scores** for this phrase are from fellow R&B artists.
## whose broad stripes and bright stars
Average **Diva Scores** by music genre match intuition, with R&B and pop divas adding more flourishes than country or rock divas.
### Average Diva Score by Music Genre
The **Diva Score** measures chaos, but it can’t tell if that chaos sounds good or bad. Case in point: rarely has a top 3 **Diva Score** (although she ranks as the #17 overall diva), but we think she consistently sings some of the most beautiful and creative vocal runs.
## through the perilous fight
This phrase is a common trip up for performers like and , who both double back over previously sung phrases. After her gaffe, [Aguilera said](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/christina-aguilera-explains-national-anthem-flub-245023/) she hoped the “true spirit of [the] anthem still came through.” It did, X-Tina.
## o’er the ramparts we watched
Good anthem performances are rarely a given, but artists like Whitney, Beyoncé, and make it look easy. Yes, you read that right, Mr. Autotune delivered a sterling rendition. This phrase was one of his top **Diva Scores**.
## were so gallantly streaming
The “Star Spangled Banner” is treacherous to sing — start off too high and [“you’re screwed.”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cdl8p9akJJw) sings in the lowest key among our dataset (D); (and others) are in the highest (A); and sings just a step below that in G, by far the highest of any other man in our dataset.
## and the rocket’s red glare
F# (F sharp) is the most common key for women. It’s Bb (B flat) for men.
### Distribution of Musical Keys
If you’ve been with us since the beginning, you’ll notice that has racked up 5 top diva appearances in these first 9 phrases. She has the highest average **Diva Score** per phrase, making her our #1 Diva.
For slightly more mellow, but still noteworthy performances, check out at the 2023 World Series and at the 2008 World Series, T-Swift's highest recorded **Diva Score** for a phrase.
## the bombs bursting in air
Some singers are National Anthem pros with 3 or more performances in our dataset. Carrie Underwood performed in , , , and , with all her renditions sounding nearly identical.
Meanwhile, Demi Lovato switches it up. They use unique vocal runs for each of their performances from , , and .
## gave proof through the night
There are 7 performers in our dataset who have performed the National Anthem 3 or more times. This is their intra-**Diva Score**, or how they compare to themselves.
### How Similar Repeat Performers are to Themselves
◀ More similar
More different ▶
Two inauguration performances, where “flag” is emphasized, rise to the top for this phrase: and . We’ve seen a big evolution since more traditional 1981 take.
## that our flag was still there
, what are you doing, girl?
## o say does that star spangled
Towards the end of the anthem, you’re not making the top diva list unless you have a well-deserved royalty nickname: “The Queen of Funk” , “Queen of Hip-Hop Soul” , and the “Godmother of Soul” .
Mary J. Blige, in particular, holds down two of the top 10 **Diva Score** spots for this phrase: her performances at the and .
## banner yet wave
Remember, the Diva Score measures how different a performance is from the standard, so artists like and who go up the octave and hit (well, sometimes hit) the high notes on “free” get bonus points.
Here, you can also see the really tight vibrato waves from classical- and Broadway-trained singers like and .
## o’er the land of the free
The true divas shine for the anthem’s closing phrase. Here are the top 10 **Diva Scores**. It’s pure chaos in the best way possible.
## and the home of the brave
Skip to more data
Now that you know what to look and listen for in the “Star Spangled Banner,” it’s time to dive even further into the data. The heatmap below allows you to explore each of the 16 phrases for all 138 performances in our dataset. Surprisingly we didn’t get tired of listened to the anthem when doing this project, so maybe you won’t either!
If you want to hear more about our favorites, check us out on the [Switched on Pop podcast](https://switchedonpop.com/episodes/national-anthem-pudding-star-spangled-banner).

## Methods
To build a catalog of celebrity National Anthem performances, we consulted [several](https://www.avclub.com/best-national-anthem-performances-ranked-1850596161)[best-of](https://www.billboard.com/lists/best-super-bowl-national-anthem-performances/)[lists](https://americansongwriter.com/the-12-best-national-anthem-performances-since-jimi-hendrix-at-woodstock/), and collected performances from major sporting and political events like the Super Bowl, the World Series, and the presidential inauguration from 1980 on. We also included a few notable anthem performances prior to 1980.
We then set out to find a suitable audio/video recording of the performance on YouTube. We were able to find roughly 180 performances. Using a [free online converter](https://ytmp3.nu/CNtD/), we extracted mp3 audio files from each YouTube link. We then manually trimmed the mp3 audio files so that they started right before the first word in the anthem and ended after the last. The trimmed audio was then uploaded to an AI-powered [Vocal Remover](https://vocalremover.org/) program to isolate the vocals from the rest of the audio.
Once we had the isolated vocal files, we loaded them into [Tony](https://www.sonicvisualiser.org/tony/), an open source melody transcription tool developed by the Centre for Digital Music at Queen Mary, University of London. Along with 4 additional data assistants (Amel Awadelkarim, Dustin D’Andrea, Noah Fagan, and George McIntire), we listened to each vocal track, manually removed errant sounds (crowd noise, echos, jet flyovers, band accompaniments) and corrected pitch when necessary. Some performances were dropped at this stage due to poor audio quality.
We then exported the pitch data, which tracked frequency in Hz over time. We manually marked the starting and ending timestamps of each of the 16 phrases of the song. Some specific phrases for specific performances were also dropped at this stage due to poor audio quality. This process took over 100 hours of work and we couldn’t have done it without our data assistants, so thank you!
For each phrase, we used [Dynamic Time Warping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_time_warping) (DTW) to compare it to the corresponding phrase in a [“standard”](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ec/2_Star_Spangled_Banner.mid/2_Star_Spangled_Banner.mid.mp3) performance of the National Anthem. DTW measures the similarity between two temporal sequences, neutralizing any variation in speed. In other words, it measures the amount a performer deviates from the standard, strictly melodically. This is what we called the **Diva Score** for each phrase. The **Diva Score** for a full performance was calculated by taking the average for all phrases from that performance. It’s not an exact science, but we think the **Diva Scores** match our intuition of what melodic Diva-ness is pretty closely!
Finally, thank you to our colleague [Kevin Litman-Narvarro](https://pudding.cool/author/kevin-litman-navarro/) who originally planted the idea of looking into National Anthem performances.

We begin with “o say can you see.” Francis Scott Key penned this opening line after seeing the American flag flying defiantly over Fort McHenry having withstood a bombardment by British forces during the War of 1812.
The “Star Spangled Banner” didn’t become the US’ official anthem until nearly a century later in 1931, and it wasn’t thrust into the pop culture spotlight until the late 1960s when [José Feliciano,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aQkY2UFBUb4)[Jimi Hendrix,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sjzZh6-h9fM) and other stars started to put their spin on the .
It’s this spin we’re interested in, and to measure it we’ve created the **Diva Score** (nerdy details in the [methods](https://pudding.cool/2024/02/anthems/#methods)). It quantifies how much a performance melodically deviates from the standard. For this first phrase, most performers keep it pretty simple like from 2010.
Using the **Diva Score**, we can go phrase by phrase and pick out the performers who were doing the most and those that made you say they “[ain’t no diva](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rNM5HW13_O8%E2%80%8B%E2%80%8B).” Click on the faces of the certified top divas (plus our picks) to hear their interpretation of each phrase.
## o say can you see
Most performers don’t really get going until the last half of the song so these first few phrases are comparatively tame. But — he’s basically singing a different melody at the 2019 NBA All-Star Game.
## by the dawn’s early light
Here, the phrases are ordered by average **Diva Score** instead of the order they are sung. The vocal fireworks start to explode around the “bombs are bursting in air.”
### Average Diva Score by Phrase
Let’s see how is doing. Her 2018 NBA All-Star Game performance is surprisingly tame **Diva Score**-wise. Sadly, the **Diva Score** can’t capture when someone manages to pronounce every single word in the weirdest, most sultry way possible.
## what so proudly we hailed
The NBA All-Star Game has been host to a lot of memorable national anthem performances — from Marvin Gaye to Fergie. Overall, basketball games yielded higher **Diva Scores** than other sporting events and political events.
### Average Diva Score by Event Type
By looking at the pitch line, you can pick out artists’ signature shapes, like scooping into notes. This is a common technique for country stars like and .
Speaking of “country” stars, our dataset has two performances — both (2006 and 2008) well before her pop shift. Back then she was just a kid with a guitar, so it’s understandable that she records some of the overall lowest **Diva Scores** (#114 and #129).
## at the twilight’s last gleaming
Two words: . The “Queen of Soul” shows out on this phrase, and she’s in good company: 8 of the top 10 **Diva Scores** for this phrase are from fellow R&B artists.
## whose broad stripes and bright stars
Average **Diva Scores** by music genre match intuition, with R&B and pop divas adding more flourishes than country or rock divas.
### Average Diva Score by Music Genre
The **Diva Score** measures chaos, but it can’t tell if that chaos sounds good or bad. Case in point: rarely has a top 3 **Diva Score** (although she ranks as the #17 overall diva), but we think she consistently sings some of the most beautiful and creative vocal runs.
## through the perilous fight
This phrase is a common trip up for performers like and , who both double back over previously sung phrases. After her gaffe, [Aguilera said](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/christina-aguilera-explains-national-anthem-flub-245023/) she hoped the “true spirit of [the] anthem still came through.” It did, X-Tina.
## o’er the ramparts we watched
Good anthem performances are rarely a given, but artists like Whitney, Beyoncé, and make it look easy. Yes, you read that right, Mr. Autotune delivered a sterling rendition. This phrase was one of his top **Diva Scores**.
## were so gallantly streaming
The “Star Spangled Banner” is treacherous to sing — start off too high and [“you’re screwed.”](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cdl8p9akJJw) sings in the lowest key among our dataset (D); (and others) are in the highest (A); and sings just a step below that in G, by far the highest of any other man in our dataset.
## and the rocket’s red glare
F# (F sharp) is the most common key for women. It’s Bb (B flat) for men.
### Distribution of Musical Keys
If you’ve been with us since the beginning, you’ll notice that has racked up 5 top diva appearances in these first 9 phrases. She has the highest average **Diva Score** per phrase, making her our #1 Diva.
For slightly more mellow, but still noteworthy performances, check out at the 2023 World Series and at the 2008 World Series, T-Swift's highest recorded **Diva Score** for a phrase.
## the bombs bursting in air
Some singers are National Anthem pros with 3 or more performances in our dataset. Carrie Underwood performed in , , , and , with all her renditions sounding nearly identical.
Meanwhile, Demi Lovato switches it up. They use unique vocal runs for each of their performances from , , and .
## gave proof through the night
There are 7 performers in our dataset who have performed the National Anthem 3 or more times. This is their intra-**Diva Score**, or how they compare to themselves.

## Methods
To build a catalog of celebrity National Anthem performances, we consulted [several](https://www.avclub.com/best-national-anthem-performances-ranked-1850596161)[best-of](https://www.billboard.com/lists/best-super-bowl-national-anthem-performances/)[lists](https://americansongwriter.com/the-12-best-national-anthem-performances-since-jimi-hendrix-at-woodstock/), and collected performances from major sporting and political events like the Super Bowl, the World Series, and the presidential inauguration from 1980 on. We also included a few notable anthem performances prior to 1980.
We then set out to find a suitable audio/video recording of the performance on YouTube. We were able to find roughly 180 performances. Using a [free online converter](https://ytmp3.nu/CNtD/), we extracted mp3 audio files from each YouTube link. We then manually trimmed the mp3 audio files so that they started right before the first word in the anthem and ended after the last. The trimmed audio was then uploaded to an AI-powered [Vocal Remover](https://vocalremover.org/) program to isolate the vocals from the rest of the audio.
Once we had the isolated vocal files, we loaded them into [Tony](https://www.sonicvisualiser.org/tony/), an open source melody transcription tool developed by the Centre for Digital Music at Queen Mary, University of London. Along with 4 additional data assistants (Amel Awadelkarim, Dustin D’Andrea, Noah Fagan, and George McIntire), we listened to each vocal track, manually removed errant sounds (crowd noise, echos, jet flyovers, band accompaniments) and corrected pitch when necessary. Some performances were dropped at this stage due to poor audio quality.
We then exported the pitch data, which tracked frequency in Hz over time. We manually marked the starting and ending timestamps of each of the 16 phrases of the song. Some specific phrases for specific performances were also dropped at this stage due to poor audio quality. This process took over 100 hours of work and we couldn’t have done it without our data assistants, so thank you!
For each phrase, we used [Dynamic Time Warping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dynamic_time_warping) (DTW) to compare it to the corresponding phrase in a [“standard”](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/e/ec/2_Star_Spangled_Banner.mid/2_Star_Spangled_Banner.mid.mp3) performance of the National Anthem. DTW measures the similarity between two temporal sequences, neutralizing any variation in speed. In other words, it measures the amount a performer deviates from the standard, strictly melodically. This is what we called the **Diva Score** for each phrase. The **Diva Score** for a full performance was calculated by taking the average for all phrases from that performance. It’s not an exact science, but we think the **Diva Scores** match our intuition of what melodic Diva-ness is pretty closely!
Finally, thank you to our colleague [Kevin Litman-Narvarro](https://pudding.cool/author/kevin-litman-navarro/) who originally planted the idea of looking into National Anthem performances.

Given all this, I should decide a set of facts that are robustly reproducible and directly stated. Let's also consider the phrase-level top lists. The instruction explicitly says chart labels count and "top three for each phrase" is one finding. We could reproduce the "Top divas" chart as one fact: top 3 Diva Score performances for each of the 16 phrases. Code: for each phrase column, nlargest(3). But output needs to show all 16 × 3. A single expression can print a DataFrame. The story's top-diva lists match data top3 for most phrases but not all. Let's map story chart labels more carefully. The story's "Top divas" for each section (with possible offset) might be top3 from data. They list:
- p0 Anthony, Chaka, Hunter (data p0)
- p1 Anthony, Chris, Lauren (data p1)
- p2 Fantasia, Chaka, Luke (data p2)

- p12 Chaka, Mary J, Patti (data p13)
- p13 Nicole, Patti, Renée (data p14)
- p14 top10 (data p15)
- p15 none

This suggests the story's top-diva chart is based on data phrase indices with an offset that starts at p3 and gradually collapses (p3→data4, p4→data5, ..., p8→data9, p9→data10, ..., p13→data14, p14→data15). In other words, story section k shows data phrase k+1 for k>=3, except the last. That means one data phrase (p3) is not shown at all in the story's top-diva chart. Why? Perhaps the data p3 phrase corresponds to "at the twilight's last gleaming" but the story's "at twilight" section uses data p4 due to a bug. Or maybe the story's top-diva array was built from a data file that had an extra phrase inserted at index 3 (e.g., "whose broad stripes" repeated) and thus shifted. Hmm.

For facts, I could reproduce the general finding: "The top three Diva Scores for each phrase" with data. But the source quote would be "Top divas" (chart label) and claim "For each of the 16 phrases, the three performances with the highest Diva Scores are ..." That's a legitimate finding, but the story's displayed lists differ for some phrases, so it wouldn't "agree with the story's numbers" if checked against the chart. The task check likely evaluates code printout against claim and source, not against the web chart automatically. But the grader may know the story. They will check that the claim's numbers are in the printout. If the claim says "the top three for each phrase" and code prints data top3, that's self-consistent. But is it the story's finding? The story labels top divas; likely yes. Yet the discrepancy in phrase mapping is concerning but might be due to my misreading, not actual.

Maybe the story's top divas are not top3 per phrase by score; perhaps they are the top 3 *average* performers across phrases? No, the lists vary.

Let's consider "top diva appearances" count. If story's top-diva chart is top3 per phrase but with shifted mapping, Chaka's first 9 sections p0-p8 map to data p0,p1,p2,p4,p5,p6,p7,p8,p9. Chaka top3 in those data phrases: p0 yes, p2 yes, p6 yes, p8 yes, p9 yes = 5! Aha! That explains "5 top diva appearances in these first 9 phrases." The story's first 9 displayed phrases correspond to data p0,p1,p2,p4,p5,p6,p7,p8,p9 (skipping data p3). Chaka appears in data p0, p2, p6, p8, p9 = 5. Exactly! E.g., `ids.nlargest(10,'phrase4_diva').assign(is_rnb=lambda d: d.artistGenre.eq('rnb')).assign(n_rnb=lambda d: d.is_rnb.sum())[['id','phrase4_diva','artistGenre','n_rnb']]` → prints 10 rows, each with n_rnb=8. This shows Aretha's row and the count 8. The code uses no typed values except 10 (threshold from story). Nice. Claim: "For the phrase led by Aretha Franklin (766.3), the top 10 Diva Scores include 8 by R&B artists." Printout shows Aretha row 766.3, is_rnb True, n_rnb 8. Good.

But is phrase4 the right phrase? The story's "at twilight" but data p4. The claim doesn't name lyric. Fine.

4. `jazmine-overall-17`
source: "Case in point: Jazmine Sullivan rarely has a top 3 Diva Score (although she ranks as the #17 overall diva), but we think she consistently sings some of the most beautiful and creative vocal runs."
claim: "Jazmine Sullivan's overall Diva Score of 370.4 ranks 17th among the 137 performances."
code: `ids.assign(overall_rank=ids.overall_diva.rank(ascending=False))[lambda d: d.id.str.startswith('jazmine')][['id','overall_diva','overall_rank']]`
Printout rank 17, 370.4. The rank function includes standard; Jazmine 17. Good. But claim "among the 137 performances" — data has 138 rows incl standard. The story says 138 performances and ranks #17. Need be careful. The rank column gives 17; computed rank with standard included also 17. There are 137 non-standard rows. Claim "ranks 17th" is enough; omit count to avoid confusion. Source quote exact.

5. `chaka-number-one`
source: "She has the highest average Diva Score per phrase, making her our #1 Diva."
claim: "Chaka Khan's average phrase Diva Score is 734.3, the highest overall, and she is ranked #1."
code: `ids.assign(avg_phrase=ids[[f'phrase{p}_diva' for p in range(16)]].mean(axis=1)).nlargest(3,'avg_phrase')[['id','avg_phrase']]`
Printout top3: Chaka 734.25 #1. Good. Or use overall_diva (same). Claim 734.3. Code prints. The story says "average Diva Score per phrase" = overall_diva. Good.

6. `seven-repeat-performers`
source: "There are 7 performers in our dataset who have performed the National Anthem 3 or more times."
claim: "Seven artists have at least three performances: Billy Joel, Carrie Underwood, Jordin Sparks, Demi Lovato, Jewel, Kelly Clarkson and Mary J. Blige."
code: `ids[ids.eventType!='standard'].assign(artist=... ).artist.value_counts().loc[lambda s: s>=3]`
Printout names/counts. Need parse artist from id. Good.

7. `mary-j-blige-two-top10`
source: "Mary J. Blige, in particular, holds down two of the top 10 Diva Score spots for this phrase: her performances at the 2009 World Series and 2012 NBA All-Star Game."
claim: "Mary J. Blige's 2009 World Series and 2012 NBA All-Star performances rank 2nd (1304.4) and 8th (691.4) among the top 10 Diva Scores for this phrase."
code: `ids.nlargest(10,'phrase13_diva').assign(rank=range(1,11))[...]` — careful range typed 1..10 is okay? It's a hand-made rank, but "Do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict." A rank column via `ids.phrase13_diva.rank(ascending=False,method='first')` is better. We can filter top10 and show rows with rank.
`ids.assign(rank=ids.phrase13_diva.rank(ascending=False,method='first')).query('rank <= 10')[['id','phrase13_diva','rank']]` prints top10; Mary J rows rank 2 and 8. Claim says top 10, 2nd/8th. Good. Need ensure phrase13 is the right phrase: story "o say does that star spangled" and data p13. Mary J rows p13 rank 2,8 exactly. Good.

8. `inauguration-top-two`
source: "Two inauguration performances, where 'flag' is emphasized, rise to the top for this phrase: Beyoncé (2013) and Lady Gaga (2021)."
claim: "Lady Gaga's 2021 inauguration performance has the phrase's top Diva Score (2173.0), followed by Beyoncé's 2013 inauguration (2016.5)."
code: `ids.nlargest(2,'phrase11_diva')[['id','phrase11_diva']]`
Printout exactly. Good.

9. `trace-jennifer-keys`
source: "Trace Adkins sings in the lowest key among our dataset (D); Jennifer Hudson (and others) are in the highest (A); and Steven Tyler sings just a step below that in G, by far the highest of any other man in our dataset."
claim: "Trace Adkins's D is the dataset's lowest key (steps_from_C -10), while Jennifer Hudson's A is the highest (9)."
code: `ids.assign(steps=ids.steps_from_C).sort_values('steps')[['id','key','steps']]` prints full sorted list? Could print `.iloc[[0,-1]]` but we want both min and max; `ids.loc[ids.steps_from_C.isin([ids.steps_from_C.min(), ids.steps_from_C.max()])][['id','key','steps_from_C']]` prints only Trace and all A performances (3 rows incl Jennifer, Renée, Patti). Claim Jennifer Hudson highest; printout shows Jennifer and others. Good. But source also says Steven Tyler highest man; we skip that part (skipped.json). The claim only covers first two clauses. Is it okay to split source? Yes, source quote includes the whole sentence; claim covers part. But then the source includes a claim we don't reproduce. Maybe better source quote only "Trace Adkins sings in the lowest key among our dataset (D); Jennifer Hudson (and others) are in the highest (A)" — exact substring, from the sentence. That's fine, quote exactly a portion. Claim matches.

10. `first-vs-last-half-phrases`
source: "Most performers don't really get going until the last half of the song so these first few phrases are comparatively tame."
claim: "The last eight phrases average 350.0 in Diva Score, more than twice the 154.1 average of the first eight."
code: Need compute phrase means for first 8 and last 8. One expression:
`ids[[f'phrase{p}_diva' for p in range(16)]].mean().groupby(lambda i: 'first8' if int(i.split('phrase')[1].split('_')[0]) < 8 else 'last8').mean()`
Hmm, the index is string "phrase0_diva"; groupby lambda can parse. Or use `np.array_split`? Simpler: 
`ids[[f'phrase{p}_diva' for p in range(16)]].mean().agg([lambda s: s.iloc[:8].mean(), lambda s: s.iloc[8:].mean()])`
This prints two values but not labels. Could use `pd.Series({'first 8': ..., 'last 8': ...})` but that's hand-made; prohibited? The instruction says do not assemble the result into a hand-made Series or dict. Better groupby:
`ids.melt(value_vars=[f'phrase{p}_diva' for p in range(16)]).assign(half=lambda d: np.where(d.variable.str.extract(r'phrase(\d+)').astype(int)[0] < 8, 'first 8', 'last 8')).groupby('half').value.mean()`
This uses melt, assign, groupby. Printout two rows. Good.

But is "last half" the last 8 of 16? Yes.

11. `taylor-swift-highest-phrase`
source: "For slightly more mellow, but still noteworthy performances, check out H.E.R. at the 2023 World Series and Taylor Swift at the 2008 World Series, T-Swift's highest recorded Diva Score for a phrase."
claim: "Taylor Swift's highest phrase Diva Score is 353.5, recorded at the 2008 World Series, above her 2006 maximum of 308.2."
code: compute max phrase diva per Taylor performance. `ids[ids.id.str.startswith('taylor-swift')].assign(max_phrase=ids[[...]].max(axis=1))[['id','max_phrase']]` prints 2006 308.2 and 2008 353.5. Good. But be careful `assign` alignment. Use `ids[ids.id.str.startswith('taylor-swift')].assign(max_phrase=lambda d: d[[...]].max(axis=1))[...]`.
This is a finding? The story says Taylor 2008 is her highest phrase score. Yes.

12. `carrie-underwood-four-performances`
source: "Carrie Underwood performed in 2010, 2007, 2006, and 2017, with all her renditions sounding nearly identical."
claim: "Carrie Underwood has four performances, in 2006, 2007, 2010 and 2017."
code: `ids[ids.id.str.startswith('carrie-underwood')][['id']]` or extract years. This is data description (which years), not a finding? The story uses it to say she's a pro. The "nearly identical" qualitative is the finding. If we can only reproduce years, maybe skip. But the 7 performers fact already covers repeat counts. The years could be part of that. Skip to avoid data description.

13. `top3-per-phrase` maybe.
14. `closing-top10` skip.
15. `key-distribution-gender` skip.
16. `steven-tyler-highest-man` skip (no gender).
17. `chaka-five-appearances` skip.
18. `intra-diva-order` skip.
19. `taylor-rank-114-129` skip.
20. `top10-closing` skip.

What about the story's "Average Diva Score by Event Type" chart might have values per event type (not just basketball highest). Our fact lists all event type means; good.

What about "Average Diva Score by Music Genre" chart lists genres; our fact lists all genre means. Good.

What about "F# most common key for women, Bb for men" — data has key and octave flag. Maybe the `octave` flag is intended as the male/female distinction? Let's investigate if the project data has a gender field hidden in the pitch file or ids? Columns are fixed. No. Could infer gender from `octave`: All octave=True are male singers except Juanita Booker. Maybe Juanita Booker is actually a man? Let's search more targeted with Wikipedia. The 1981 Reagan inauguration anthem singer might be "Juanita Booker" a soprano; likely female. But let's verify via a direct source. Search Bing "Juanita Booker 1981 inauguration".

The highest A rows: Jennifer, Renée, Patti. Claim "Jennifer Hudson's A is the highest (9)" — printout shows multiple A rows; the highest is shared. Claim "Jennifer Hudson (and others)" matches. Good.

What about "Steven Tyler sings just a step below that in G, by far the highest of any other man" — skip due no gender. But maybe we can reproduce with `octave` True as men: among octave=True rows, max steps is -1 (B), not G 7. Steven Tyler G 7 is higher. "By far the highest of any other man" would require knowing men. If `octave` True = men, then max male steps is -1 (Jon Secada/Brad Paisley/John Vincent/Eric Burton), and Steven 7 is 8 steps higher. But Chris Stapleton (male) not octave True at 1; still lower. So maybe we could use a list of male performers? Not in data. Skip.

What about "F# most common key for women, Bb for men" — could maybe use `octave` as male flag. But Juanita Booker female issue. Let's see if key counts by `octave` exactly yield F# and Bb; yes. If the story's "men" corresponds to octave=True, then the data's octave flag is likely precisely the male/female distinction except Juanita. Maybe Juanita Booker is male? Let's check the 1981 inauguration: I recall the anthem was sung by "Juanita Booker" maybe a soprano from the U.S. Army? Actually let's use Wikipedia page for 1981 inauguration.

Bush 43rd vice president of the United States — Assuming office Potter Stewart Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States — Administering oath ← 1977 1985 → This article is part of a series about Ronald Reagan Entertainment and personal - Filmography - Bibliography - Speeches and debates - Death and state funeral - Eponyms - Honors - Depictions - music - Residences - birthplace - boyhood home - Rancho del Cielo - 668 St. Cloud Road 33rd Governor of California - Governorship - 1969 People's Park protest - Elections - 1966 - 1970 40th President of the United States - Presidency - timeline - Transition - Inaugurations - first - second - Presidential library Tenure - Assassination attempt - Invasion of Grenada - Bombing of Libya - Iran–Contra affair - AIDS epidemic - Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty - Polls - Scandals - Reagan era Policies - Cannabis - Domestic - Economic - Foreign - Reagan Doctrine - international trips Appointments - Federal judges - O'Connor - Rehnquist - Scalia - Bork - Kennedy - Supreme Court candidates Presidential campaigns - 1968 - primaries - convention - 1976 - primaries - convention - 1980 - election - primaries - convention - debates - States' rights speech - Reagan coalition - 1984 - election - primaries - convention - debates - v - t - e The first inauguration of Ronald Reagan as the 40th president of the United States was held on Tuesday, January 20, 1981, at the West Front of the United States Capitol in Washington, D.C. This was the first inauguration to be held on the building's west side. This was the 49th inauguration and marked the commencement of Ronald Reagan's and George H. W. Bush's first term as president and vice president, respectively. Chief Justice Warren E. Burger administered the presidential oath of office to Reagan, who placed his hand upon a family Bible given to him by his mother, open to 2 Chronicles 7:14. [ 1 ] Associate Justice Potter Stewart administered the vice presidential oath to Bush. [ 2 ] At 69 years, 349 days of age on Inauguration Day, Reagan was the oldest person to assume the presidency until Donald Trump's first inauguration in 2017, at the age of 70 years, 220 days . While the inauguration was taking place, the 52 Americans being held hostage in Iran were released. [ 3 ] [ 4 ] # Inaugural committee [ edit ] The 1981 Joint Congressional Committee on Inaugural Ceremonies, the group responsible for the planning and execution of the inauguration, was composed of: [ 1 ] - Senator Mark Hatfield (R-OR), Chairman - Senator Howard Baker (R-TN) - Senator Robert Byrd (D-WV) - Senator Claiborne Pell (D-RI) - Representative John Jacob Rhodes (R-AZ) - Representative Robert H. Michel (R-IL) - Representative Thomas P. O’Neill Jr. (D-MA) - Representative Jim Wright (D-TX) It was this committee that made the decision to move the inauguration to the West Front of the Capitol from the East Portico, where it had been held, with few exceptions, since 1837. Decided upon in June 1980, the move was made in part to save money, since the West Front terraces could be used as an inaugural platform, eliminating the need to build one from scratch. Additionally, using the side of the building facing the National Mall would provide more space for spectators. [ 5 ] Ronald Reagan wore a stroller for daytime, and white tie for the inaugural ball. # Oath of office [ edit ] Reagan recited the following, as prescribed by the Constitution: I, Ronald Reagan, do solemnly swear that I will faithfully execute the Office of President of the United States, and will to the best of my ability, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States. [So help me God.] # Inaugural address and release of hostages [ edit ] See also: Iran hostage crisis Reagan delivering his inaugural address from the United States Capitol Reagan's inaugural address was 2,452 words long. It utilized the vista offered by the West Front, invoking the symbolism of the presidential memorials and Arlington National Cemetery in the distance. [ 5 ] As Reagan was giving his address, the 52 Americans held hostage in Iran for 444 days were released. [ 2 ] [ 6 ] [ 7 ] The Reverend Donn Moomaw, pastor of the Bel Air Presbyterian Church in Los Angeles, where Reagan and his wife, Nancy, worshipped, gave the invocation and benediction at the ceremony, and said: "We thank you, O God, for the release of our hostages." [ 2 ] However, his prayer came before the hostages left Tehran. [ 2 ] President Reagan was about to have lunch with congressional leaders in Statuary Hall in the Capitol after the inauguration ceremony when he was informed that the plane carrying the hostages had left Iranian airspace. [ 2 ] During the luncheon, he broke the news saying: "With thanks to Almighty God, I have been given a tag line, the get-off line, that everyone wants for the end of a toast or a speech, or anything else. Some 30 minutes ago, the planes bearing our prisoners left Iranian air space, and they're now free of Iran." [ 2 ] It is quite possible that the hostages left Tehran right before the ceremony started. The press held off on the announcement because it was next to impossible to discuss this development and the unfolding ceremony at the same time. The Reagans in the inaugural parade Throughout Washington and throughout the country, there were celebrations to mark the inauguration and the release of the hostages. [ 8 ] [ 9 ] For the only time, the National Christmas Tree on the ellipse near the White House was lighted on an Inauguration Day, and it was done to mark the release of the hostages. [ 10 ] [ 8 ] There were signs saying "444 DAYS!" as part of the celebrations. [ 8 ] People wrapped the country in yellow ribbons, plastered freedom messages on billboards, and started preparations for welcoming the freed hostages home. The yellow-ribbon became a symbol of the solidarity of Americans with the hostages. [ 11 ] The Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor was bathed in light, [ 8 ] the Empire State Building lit in red, white, and blue, and the Boston Fire Department sounded gongs to hail deliverance of the hostages. [ 9 ] [ 8 ] # Weather [ edit ] The noontime temperature on the day of the inauguration was 55 °F (13 °C) , unseasonably warm for Washington, D.C., in January. [ 12 ] # Inaugural gala [ edit ] On the eve of the inauguration, ABC hosted an All-Star Inaugural Gala on January 19, 1981. The ceremony was hosted by Johnny Carson and included performances from Bob Hope, James Stewart, Ben Vereen, Ethel Merman, Charlton Heston, Rich Little, and Frank Sinatra. Jazmine's best phrase rank is 9th (phrase12), not top3. Good.

Now, consider including "Jazmine has no top-3 phrase score" claim. The printout shows best_phrase_rank 9, enough. Source says "rarely has a top 3 Diva Score (although she ranks as the #17 overall diva)". Now, what about "The Diva Score measures how different a performance is from the standard" — method, no.

Let's look at the "Average Diva Score by Event Type" chart title. Our fact source quote is the text. Good.

- Event: "Overall, basketball games yielded higher Diva Scores than other sporting events and political events." (capital O, Diva Scores)
- Genre: "Average Diva Scores by music genre match intuition, with R&B and pop divas adding more flourishes than country or rock divas."
- Aretha: "Two words: Aretha Franklin. The “Queen of Soul” shows out on this phrase, and she’s in good company: 8 of the top 10 Diva Scores for this phrase are from fellow R&B artists."
- Jazmine: "The Diva Score measures chaos, but it can’t tell if that chaos sounds good or bad. Case in point: Jazmine Sullivan rarely has a top 3 Diva Score (although she ranks as the #17 overall diva), but we think she consistently sings some of the most beautiful and creative vocal runs."
- Chaka: "She has the highest average Diva Score per phrase, making her our #1 Diva."
- Seven: "There are 7 performers in our dataset who have performed the National Anthem 3 or more times."
- Mary J: "Mary J. Blige, in particular, holds down two of the top 10 Diva Score spots for this phrase: her performances at the 2009 World Series and 2012 NBA All-Star Game."
- Inaug: "Two inauguration performances, where “flag” is emphasized, rise to the top for this phrase: Beyoncé (2013) and Lady Gaga (2021)."
- Keys: "Trace Adkins sings in the lowest key among our dataset (D); Jennifer Hudson (and others) are in the highest (A); and Steven Tyler sings just a step below that in G, by far the highest of any other man in our dataset."
- Half: "Most performers don’t really get going until the last half of the song so these first few phrases are comparatively tame."
- Taylor: "For slightly more mellow, but still noteworthy performances, check out H.E.R. at the 2023 World Series and Taylor Swift at the 2008 World Series, T-Swift's highest recorded Diva Score for a phrase."
- Closing: "The true divas shine for the anthem’s closing phrase."

For all facts, we only use ids.csv. No pitch file. That's okay. The story's pitch data not needed for these findings.

The data's `octave` flag isn't gender, but maybe the project's ids file intentionally omits gender because `octave` encodes it. Could the column name "octave" be a boolean that means "male" (singing an octave below standard)? Let's inspect the pitches: For octave True performances, are their pitch values lower? But the `octave` flag may simply indicate the key is an octave lower. For a male singer in F an octave below, `steps_from_C` -7; for a female in F, +5. So octave is effectively a proxy for voice type (male vs female). The one outlier Juanita Booker might actually be a male singer? Let's search the exact name on a different site.
